summary: The note describes how students have become key contributors to historical documentation and archiving since September 2023, through projects at schools, universities and international groups. Examples include digitizing local collections, a VR archive experience, a transatlantic digitization effort, an ethics symposium, local oral histories and environmental data archiving. It argues these projects build practical, technological and ethical skills while widening access to the historical record.
one_line: Student-led archiving projects since September 2023 build practical, technological and ethical skills while digitizing and preserving local, global and environmental history.
key_facts: The "Living Chronicles" project was launched on September 15, 2023, by students at the Belmont Historical Society in collaboration with Hamilton Secondary School.
Mrs. Eleanor Richardson, a history teacher, guided high school seniors in digitizing and cataloging early 20th century diaries, letters, and photographs for "Living Chronicles".
"Living Chronicles" used high-resolution scanning and advanced metadata tagging to make archives more accessible to researchers and the public.
The University of Midtown's Department of History, led by Dr. Henry Carter, introduced a semester-long archiving workshop on November 1, 2023, for undergraduates.
Dr. Carter's workshop moves from identifying and classifying documents, to conservation, to digital archiving.

On December 6, 2023, graduate students from the Franklin Institute of Technology unveiled a virtual reality (VR) experience based on the institution's archives, led by James Anderson and Maria Gonzalez.

The "Transatlantic Memories" initiative was established on January 10, 2024, by the Global Historical Studies Group, with participants from universities including Cambridge and the University of Capetown, to digitize letters, ship logs, and images on trade, migration, and cultural exchange.

The Ethics in Archiving symposium was held on February 2, 2024, with students from several local universities discussing privacy rights, representation of marginalized groups, and repatriation of artifacts to their countries of origin.
The "Hometown Histories" initiative, launched on March 3, 2024, by Emerson College students, digitizes local newspapers and conducts oral history interviews with community elders.

In April 2024, undergraduate researchers from Bentley University presented a project archiving over a century of meteorological data and environmental studies at the Environmental Historical Society's annual conference.
The Bentley University work gave insights into climate change patterns and ecological shifts, showing archives can inform current environmental policies.
